claims.text: Google SRE defines five AI autonomy levels (L0 Manual, L1 Assisted, L2 Partial, L3 High, L4 Full) across the functions Monitor, Investigate, Mitigate, Actuate and Self Direct.
Under Google's Progressive Authorization, agents start at Level 2 autonomy, where they investigate, propose and stage mitigations but need explicit human approval to execute.
Google agents advance to L3 or L4 only for specific, well-bounded scenarios after sustained, statistically significant success rates against human-verified Golden evaluation data.
Google's AI Operator currently runs at L2 (human SRE reviews and accepts mitigation suggestions for critical operations) and at L3, where it executes mitigations autonomously for minor incidents.
Google's AI Operator has run across thousands of incidents, with every execution trace stored in Spanner and evaluated with an LLM-as-a-Judge against Golden Data.
Google runs nightly evaluations on its Everest evaluation platform against a rolling dataset of recent real incidents, combining LLM-as-a-Judge raters with strict deterministic scoring.
Google's Gemini-powered CLI can initiate policy-compliant mitigations such as traffic drains, gated by a central Mitigation Safety Verification Service.

Google's Actuation Agent provides a curated, dynamically filtered registry of mitigation tools (e.g. traffic draining, capacity upsizing) and turns an agent's EvaluateAction request into a concrete, verifiable execution plan.

Meta's root-cause system uses a two-stage architecture: heuristic retrieval, code ownership and runtime code graph traversal cut thousands of changes to a few hundred, then an LLM ranker identifies the root cause.
Meta's RCA system measured 42% accuracy at investigation creation time on its web monorepo, and it suppresses low-confidence answers rather than misleading engineers.
Meta's Diff Risk Score uses AI to predict the risk of code changes at the diff/PR stage to inform merge and gating decisions before release.

Google Cloud's Alert Triage Agent (announced at Cloud Next '25) analyzes each alert's context, gathers information and renders a verdict along with a history of its evidence and decisions, enabling audit of the reasoning.

Google's SRE materials describe fetch_playbook as a function call in an internal agentic framework, so the agent retrieves an approved runbook as a tool-style operation rather than running freeform commands.
Cleric uses graduated autonomy by problem type: per-problem-class accuracy scores decide where the agent acts independently and where it escalates to an engineer with a recommendation and evidence.
Cleric verifies outcomes in a closed loop by triangulating after the fact: whether the alert recurred, whether downstream services stabilized, and whether the engineer overrode the fix.
Cleric captures decision traces from investigations, corrections and follow-up actions, reinforcing patterns that led to verified outcomes and discarding others.

Per Cleric's own report, Traversal verification is open-loop (no automated check that the inferred causal chain matched the true root cause), Resolve is designed for autonomous remediation against pre-defined workflows, and Traversal does investigation only with no remediation.
Cleric is read-only by design and explicitly declines to remediate, reporting about five minutes to root cause on average, so the fix is still executed manually.

Resolve AI executes fixes without human intervention for well-defined incident patterns under a graduated trust model, using a knowledge graph of code commits, infrastructure topology and incident histories.
Resolve.ai's stated goal is to take 80% of incidents to resolution without human intervention, with confidence thresholds, scoped permissions and audit trails as failure-safety design.
Resolve.ai runs a multi-agent architecture that investigates several hypotheses in parallel, with write actions placed behind engineer approval.
Traversal builds a Production World Model and a Causal Search Engine that traverses 10+ hops to locate root causes, delivering findings for human action rather than autonomous execution.
PagerDuty's Spring 2026 release added an SRE Agent that can be placed on on-call schedules and escalation policies like a human responder, triaging and diagnosing before paging a human.

Self-healing systems commonly use a three-tier escalation (auto-heal via restarts/rollbacks, alert-and-propose with human approval, then page on-call), with restart-loop prevention that escalates when a process oscillates faster than the cooldown window.

Safe autonomous remediation requires idempotent actions, pre-defined rollback plans, audit logs and human approval for state-mutating writes, with starting points such as restarting a single stateless instance or rolling back a feature flag with health gating.
